paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: But what's the other thing we're going to do? I'll tell you that in a second. I want to give you a little bit of a preview of where does this all come from? Here's our friend Je Tsongkapa. 14th century. What are his dates? Every Buddhist password in our organization. Whatever his dates — Sandra, you're way too fast, you should have waited for the money — okay, 1357 to 1419. Incredible scholar, incredible practitioner.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And in 1921, a teacher who we call Pabongka Rinpoche gave a 24-day teaching on the steps of the path, the Lam Rim, where he outlined all of those steps, basing his teaching primarily — not entirely, but primarily — on Je Tsongkapa's Lam Rim Chenmo. He gave a 24-day oral teaching. You can imagine it was probably about eight to 10 hours a day of teaching in a lecture hall — several hundred people, I think they say something like 700-ish people showed up, no microphones. And he gave an extraordinary teaching on all the steps of the path.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And in that teaching, he taught all the steps. And then near the end, he focused on meditation — all the things you need to do, now that you've learned the entire steps on the path, all the way from the beginning through the lower, medium, and higher scopes, all the realizations. And then he said, "Okay, guys, good job. Now I'm going to teach you how to meditate." And he spent a whole day teaching everyone all the things you need to know on how to meditate. And then near the last day, he taught all about emptiness. So he gave the key elements of meditation — shamatha — and emptiness — vipashyana — and merged those two together at the very end and said, "Okay, now everyone go home, have a nice life, and meditate on all the steps of the path. Good luck." I'm sure it wasn't quite as sarcastic as that. But he was like, "All right, I've given you everything. Now here are your tools." The tools that you take into all of those steps are going to be your meditation and your growing understanding of emptiness — your growing wisdom that will grow as you meditate on the steps on the path. He created an amazing package to go from the beginning to the end. And throughout, he also mixed in the secret teachings with the open teachings, so that if you have the karma to hear it, you can start being able to incorporate those different practices all together.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So the way that this was originally taught by Geshe Michael — and the way that I'm going to do this, because I've actually found this to be the most helpful — is we're going to go to the end of the book. We're going to go to day 21 and start with how to meditate. Because if we can learn how to develop this tool — and meditation is a tool. It's a method. It's a microscope. It's an activity that we do whose results have the power to completely change who you are.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: In arriving at a single point in meditation, even without deeper realizations — even without being able to understand emptiness all that well — you can really change the way that you help people just by learning how to meditate, and to meditate well, and meditate correctly. And that's why, in the advertising, you might've seen the words "transformational meditation." Everyone in the world is selling meditation right now. And does your meditation work? Do you understand the causes for meditation? Do you understand how to create the conditions for good meditation — for a good meditation session, for a good meditation place? But more importantly, do you understand how to create the causes to even be able to meditate?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: There are deeper causes, and then there are surface causes — like, "Oh yeah, tell your kids not to talk while you're meditating for your hour." Okay, does that work? Tell your family to shut up during your meditation hour. Does that work? Tell the birds outside to shut up. Tell the garbage truck to shut up. Tell your mind to shut up. How about that? Have you ever tried to tell your mind to shut up? "Stop obsessing about that, Tim. Forget it. Stop thinking about that. Stop creating those stories. Stop creating things that don't exist in your mind." Oh, good job. So how do we learn about those deeper causes so we can meditate?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And then how do we turn that microscope on the object of emptiness? That's the second chapter. How do we go into that, focusing on the lack of self-nature? How do we focus on the fact that nothing is not coming from how you treated others in the past? And so all of those things together become the key tools that you can then move into understanding the steps on the path and being able to apply them in your life.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: If you can meditate well, and you can focus on the challenges that you have, you can start seeing the nature of those challenges. You can start seeing the causes behind what's in front of you. What seems like the cause is not actually the cause. The thing that you're doing to solve the problem isn't actually solving the problem. Your self-cherishing, your incorrect views — all of these things are built into the mechanism of us so innately that, to unwind them, we need the tools. We need those tools to make them visible, to be able to see things that we couldn't see before. And how do we do that? We have to do it through meditation, through concentration, through kindness.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So what's our other goal here? There's still plenty of goals. So Pabongka Rinpoche did this — oops, hold on — so Pabongka Rinpoche taught this in an oral way, in a big room, lots of people. They did not have Zoom, obviously. They did not have voice recorders. They didn't even have microphones, which means they didn't have cameras. So Pabongka Rinpoche's student, Trijang Rinpoche, wrote the book down — took notes — and then spent a large part of his life writing the book down, writing the details down, talking with his teacher, making sure he got everything correct. So he took the outline of the class, the 24 days, and created an enormous book of something like 400 folios in Tibetan, and then left us a written record of Pabongka Rinpoche's Lam Rim.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And this has been translated by several people into various languages. A fellow student of Geshe Michael's, Art Engle, translated this book. It's actually in three volumes. It's a wonderful resource. Why am I saying that? So there are resources available already in translation. And Geshe Michael has taught this.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So Khen Rinpoche taught his students. Geshe Lobsang Tharchin — Khen Rinpoche — left Tibet, escaped, and then ended up in a monastery in northern New Jersey, United States, a Mongolian monastery. And then he spent the rest of his life teaching. He just taught. And that's actually where Geshe Michael met him. He has been teaching extensively since about 1993 — actually started before that — but has been actively teaching his entire life as well. So that's the lineage of the teachings.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So back in 2010, Geshe Michael started teaching the Lam Rim, starting with Pabongka Rinpoche's text. He was taught it three times by his teacher. And now he's passing on the lineage to us. 95% of the way done. And now we're going back to the beginning, because now it's time to teach it again.
